chief_complaint: kidney stones, bone pain, fatigue, and depression found on routine checkup
hpi_details: 62F found to have persistent hypercalcemia on routine lab work. Reports 2-year history of recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, diffuse bone aches, constipation, lethargy, and mild depression ('bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans').
ideas: thinks her kidney stones are just from drinking tap water
concerns: worried her bone pain is due to osteoporosis or cancer
expectations: wants to get rid of her kidney stones and feel energetic again

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Hyperparathyroidism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Perform parathyroid localization imaging (Sestamibi scan + neck ultrasound), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: kidney stones, bone pain, fatigue, and depression found on routine checkup

Key HPI features: 62F found to have persistent hypercalcemia on routine lab work. Reports 2-year history of recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, diffuse bone aches, constipation, lethargy, and mild depression ('bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans').

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 70, BP 138/84. Exam unremarkable except mild epigastric tenderness. Bloods: Serum total Calcium 11.8 mg/dL, Ionized Calcium elevated, Phosphate low (2.1 mg/dL), Intact PTH inappropriately elevated (145 pg/mL), 25-OH Vitamin D normal. 24-hour urine calcium elevated (>300 mg/day). DEXA scan shows osteoporosis at distal radius.
Relevant background/PMH: Recurrent nephrolithiasis, osteopenia, hypertension
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe confusion or very high calcium — hypercalcemic crisis needing urgent hydration.
management_principles: Perform parathyroid localization imaging (Sestamibi scan + neck ultrasound)
Refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy
Encourage adequate oral hydration and avoid loop/thiazide diuretic shifts until surgical evaluation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

DEXA scan shows osteoporosis at distal radius.
reference_soap.assessment: Primary Hyperparathyroidism secondary to solitary parathyroid adenoma.
reference_soap.plan: Perform parathyroid localization imaging (Sestamibi scan + neck ultrasound). Refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy. Encourage adequate oral hydration and avoid thiazide diuretics, which can worsen hypercalcemia.

learning_objectives: Identify classic clinical manifestations of primary hyperparathyroidism
Interpret lab profile (elevated calcium, low phosphate, elevated intact PTH)
Differentiate primary hyperparathyroidism from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)
List surgical indications for asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism

teaching.one_liner: A parathyroid adenoma overproduces PTH, causing the classic tetrad of 'bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones' — bone pain, kidney stones, constipation, and depression from chronic hypercalcemia.
red_flags: Severe confusion or very high calcium — hypercalcemic crisis needing urgent hydration

must_ask.say: How many kidney stones have you had, and over what time period?
Where is the bone pain, and how would you describe it?
Have you had constipation or felt low in mood?
How would you describe your energy level?
Was the high calcium found on a routine blood test?

history.answer: I came in because the clinic called after my routine health checkup and told me that my calcium level was high.
They ran my routine annual blood tests last week, and the doctor told me my calcium was eleven point eight, which is above normal.
They told me my calcium was borderline high at last year's checkup too, but no one looked into it back then.
I fasted overnight for twelve hours, drank only plain water, and was feeling rested without any recent cold or heavy workouts.
I check my blood pressure at home sometimes and it usually runs around 130 to 140 over 80, but I haven't rechecked my calcium.
I have been feeling constantly exhausted and drained for the past year or two, even when I get a full night of sleep.
No, I haven't had any unusual headaches, blurred vision, or changes in my eyesight.
Yes, I feel thirsty all the time lately and I find myself waking up two or three times every night to urinate.
My weight has remained steady around 60 kilograms, and while my appetite is slightly lower, I haven't had significant weight loss.
No, I have not had any chest tightness, shortness of breath, or heart fluttering.
No, I have not experienced any weakness on one side, numbness, facial drooping, or slurred speech.
I have had two episodes of kidney stones over the past two years, and passing them was excruciatingly painful.
I have deep, dull aching in my bones, mostly in my forearms, lower legs, and hips, which has been bothering me for months.
I have been terribly constipated for over a year, only going once every three or four days and feeling uncomfortably bloated.
I frequently get a mild dull ache in the upper part of my stomach, though it never gets severe.
I've been feeling down, irritable, and mentally foggy for months, which is really out of character for me.
No, I have not had any fevers, chills, drenching night sweats, or cough.
No, I haven't noticed any lumps or swellings in my neck, armpits, or anywhere else.
My thighs feel somewhat weak when standing up from low chairs, but I haven't had muscle spasms or cramps.
No, I am not unusually sensitive to cold, and my skin and hair have seemed normal.
I was taking a water pill called chlorthalidone 25 milligrams daily for high blood pressure, but my doctor stopped it recently after the blood test.
I do not take any calcium pills, vitamin D supplements, antacids, or herbal remedies.
I eat fairly healthy meals, but I started drinking lots of tap water because I thought it would help flush out kidney stones.
I try to walk around the park three times a week, but lately my fatigue makes it tough to keep up.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I worked as a middle school teacher until I retired, so I was never exposed to chemical dust or asbestos.
I might have a sip of wine once or twice a year during celebrations, but essentially I don't drink alcohol.
I have never fractured a bone, but a bone scan two years ago showed mild thinning called osteopenia.
I reached menopause twelve years ago when I was fifty, and I have never used hormone replacement therapy.
No, I have never had tuberculosis and I have never been in close contact with anyone who had it.
Aside from the recurrent kidney stones, osteopenia, and high blood pressure, I haven't had any chronic illnesses.
I had shockwave treatment two years ago to break up a kidney stone, but I've never had major surgery or hospitalizations.
I don't have any known allergies to drugs, foods, or materials.
My parents had high blood pressure in their older years, but no one in my family had kidney stones, calcium issues, or endocrine tumors.
I live in an apartment with my husband, and my adult children live nearby.
I was wondering if all the mineral-heavy tap water I drink caused the calcium buildup and my kidney stones.
Because my bones ache so much, I've been terrified that I have advanced osteoporosis or even bone cancer.
I really hope we can treat whatever is causing these stones and body aches so I can get my energy back.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, heart rate 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert, mildly fatigued female sitting comfortably in no acute distress; height 158 cm, weight 60 kg, BMI 24.0 kg/m².
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and without palpable nodules or bruits.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory effort and no wheezes or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or carotid bruits.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without scars, distension, or visible pulsations.
Normoactive to slightly hypoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants; no abdominal bruits.
Soft with mild tenderness on deep palpation in the epigastric region; no guarding or rebound tenderness.
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly; liver edge is smooth and non-tender.
Normal thoracic and lumbar spinal curvature without kyphosis; no midline spine or paraspinal tenderness.
No pretibial edema or calf swelling in either lower extremity.
Radial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with mildly sluggish psychomotor responses but intact concentration and memory.
